title: War Crimes, Crimes Against Humanity, Genocide, and the Architecture of International Criminal Law

excerpt: International criminal law defines individual responsibility for atrocity crimes that shock the conscience of humanity. This article explains war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, aggression, contextual elements, protected interests, intent, command responsibility, superior orders, joint criminal enterprise, aiding and abetting, complementarity, universal jurisdiction, evidence, victims, witnesses, reparations, and enforcement limits. It connects the Genocide Convention, Geneva Conventions, Rome Statute, ICTY, ICTR, ICC, and hybrid tribunals to the institutional architecture that turns mass violence into legal charges, cases, judgments, and records. The article also addresses selectivity, state cooperation, immunities, arrest warrants, atrocity documentation, and the political limits of prosecution. By combining doctrine, institutions, and lawyer-facing workflows, it shows how international criminal law identifies responsible individuals without reducing collective violence to abstract state conduct alone.
